title: 1  Culture, Interdisciplinarity, and ML
text:
Abstract
Introductory overview: setting the agenda regarding getting ‘beyond ethics’ in critical thinking about ML, in favour of the necessity of developing wider interdisciplinary and structural understandings of AI/ML. Establishing music as an exemplary domain for thinking through these issues, and introducing the MusAI research program’s attempts to develop critical accounts of AI and music, and this course as a key experimental step in our work. A first lens on these issues is through recent debates on ‘AI and culture’, drawing out, via a focus on recommender systems, how culture gets into ML in several distinct ways. From this to the question of how ML applications configure human users, employing ideas from Science and Technology Studies (STS) – and asking: could it be otherwise?

title: 2  The Objects of ML
text:
Abstract
How does ML conceptualize the objects it models, such as ‘music’ in music information retrieval? Through the question of musical genre – as a particular kind of musical object – we can see radical reductions in how music is often modelled. This has epistemological consequences for what these models can tell us in research, but also quite possibly ontological consequences if – as some argue – models of social and cultural phenomena, such as music or genre, do not merely describe or predict but are performatively changing the very thing they model.

title: 3  The Political Economy of AI Music (I)
text:
Abstract
How do we think the forms of value that ML might produce, and the costs that it entails? What are the economic conditions that have enabled the recent profusion of AI music companies, and that have shaped the products and services they have developed? How does commercial music AI relate to the broader music ecosystem, and what might be the longer-term impact of their entanglement? Introduction to the political economy of AI music, and the implications it may have for the future of music cultures and music as a common resource.

title: 4  The Political Economy of AI Music (II)
text:
Abstract
In this series of videos I explore the cultures of AI music technology startups in a period of profound disruption between 2020 and 2025.
My initial focus is on how these organisations manoeuvre between the simultaneous challenges of developing new experimental technologies and building an engaged set of users, while satisfying investors and workers, while the technology, cultural and music business landscapes are also changing around them. My initial study looks at 4 companies each building generative music engines for dynamic music experiences, and I compare their different innovation strategies: how quickly they go for product-market-fit, how agile they are, and how they accumulate assets and capability that may build value even without working products. In addition, above all, I consider how they articulate their product visions as value propositions and how that lands in dialogue with music communities and investors. The research reveals a set of ways that innovation seeks to create the conditions for open-ended exploratory search which is technology-first: it seeks to develop new technology capabilities, assets and configurations, and then to experimentally discover new markets to which these capabilities can be applied.
Beyond the initial scope of the first study, I consider how the leading AI music company Suno, while having a more technologically advanced product than the companies considered above, faces similar challenges in articulating and developing its product offering and remaining agile, especially in light of recent damaging lawsuits. I also survey recent simultaneous developments in related technology areas that suggest mutual adaptation. In particular, I consider how the stem separation company Audioshake is claiming to enable conversion of legacy music into Dolby Atmos spatial formats, which may in turn influence the uptake of dynamic music experiences.
In a second study I look at the user interface design challenges of music AI companies, again developing a technology-led innovation perspective. Generative technologies are seemingly powerful creative tools but their opacity forces a set of interface design possibilities that are generally antithetical to creative practices. Through a set of music AI companies I trace interface design development as it attends to different creative user needs, focusing on some (but not all) creative users’ need for creative engagement and differentiation. This includes various design innovations that allow generative processes to be integrated with other interfaces that allow user control. I propose that creative AI companies could better employ value-centred design frameworks which centre the value of the arts, in doing so better serving their product designs and also improving the value they bring to creative arts communities.
In a third study, I look at the emerging field of training data attribution in creative AI applications. Following the widespread calls for AI companies to respect the copyright protections of training data with some legal success, there is a massive mobilisation to create AI training data attribution strategies, which are being tentatively explored by record companies and copyright agencies. I present a typology of attribution strategies and I propose that each can be analysed in terms of the their claims to underlying ‘determinants of value’, those ways that we naturally understand a cultural product to be worthy of receiving remuneration. I also consider how transparent each strategy is and how easily it can be gamed.

title: 5  ML, Public Value, and Institutional and Design Alternatives: the Case of Music Recommender Systems
text:
Abstract
With ideas around political economy, value and the user in hand, we venture beyond this to consider the limits of personalization as a paradigm, and introduce ideas of public value. Focus on a case study of a combined conceptual-and-technical intervention: a new metric for recommender systems conceived around notions of public value.

title: 6  AI, Music and Copyright
text:
Abstract
Criticism of generative AI for music is often framed in terms of copyright and the expropriation of creative labour. However, is this the productive critical perspective? (Musical) copyright, whilst heterogeneous and highly complex, tends to account for a narrow selection of musical qualities and critique on the basis of straightforward plagiarism oversimplifies the processes at work in generative systems.

7  ML and its Others: Can AI Be Decolonised?
text:
Abstract
This week explores the limitations of decolonising AI in the music industry. It questions whether AI, as a socio-technical assemblage always embedded in its larger cultural and historical contexts, is a coherent object that can be decolonised. Using the Arabic music industries based out of the UAE and Egypt, as well as Anghami, a Beirut-based music streaming service, as case studies, it demonstrates how the Arabic music industry operationalises AI in ways that both challenge and uphold relations of power within the region and beyond. Most broadly, it shows the limitations of decolonising AI even when starting from the epistemologies of listeners and musicians in the global South.

title: 8  Machine Learning and Creative Practice (I)
text:
Abstract
What kinds of technical and artistic innovation does ML enable? What is the relationship between them and how are they shaped by aesthetic concerns? Can artistic work with ML serve as a source of critique, informed by humanities scholarship? We examine contemporary and critical practice in musical composition with ML.

title: 10  AI and Artistic Critique
text:
Abstract
What is artistic critique in relation to AI, and how does it relate to other configurations of art’s relationship to technoscience — for instance ideological, demonstrative, collaborative? What use is critique generally in relation to AI and technoscience, and what use is artistic critique specifically? How does the history of AI critique in music relate to canonical philosophical and humanistic critiques of AI?
